pages.title: Executive summary — SF rent increase, Outer Sunset 94122
pages.desc: The 2023 Rent Board licence requirement is local, not state: what an individual owner must do, step by step, with the numbers for two rent-controlled units.
pages.h1: Raising rent on two 1940 flats in the Outer Sunset
pages.lede: The rule you read about is real, and it is a San Francisco local law, not a state law. It applies to an individual owner of a two-unit building exactly as it applies to a corporation. Nothing is sent to the Rent Board for approval before you notify a tenant — but the unit must be licensed on the day the increase takes effect.

blocks.head: Is the 2023 Rent Board requirement a state law or a local law?
blocks.body:
It is local. The duty sits in the San Francisco Administrative Code, Chapter 37, §37.15 — a City ordinance, titled “Reporting Obligations; Licensing” and footnoted on the City's own page as “Added by Ord. No. 265-20, effective January 18, 2021”. The Rent Board's 2023 press release describes it in exactly those terms: “A new law passed by the City and County of San Francisco.”

Why 2023 is the year you remember. The ordinance took effect in 2021, but it started on a staggered timetable. For buildings with 10 or more residential units the duty began 1 July 2022. For condominiums and buildings with fewer than 10 units — which is what a two-unit 1940 building is — the duty began 1 March 2023, with updates due every 1 March after that. The Rent Board's adopted Rule §13.14 says the same thing: for buildings with fewer than ten units it “shall only apply to rent increases that are effective on or after March 1, 2023.”

So: the licence rule is local (City ordinance); the notice rule you must also obey is state (California Civil Code §827); and the anti-discrimination rules are both state and federal. Three layers, three sources.

blocks.head: I am one individual, not a corporation. Do I still have to report and hold a licence before notifying tenants?
blocks.body:
Yes — and this is the part most owners get wrong, so read it twice.

§37.15(a) opens with “Owners of residential dwelling units subject to this Chapter 37…”. There is no individual-owner exemption, no small-landlord exemption and no two-unit exemption anywhere in the section. The Rent Board's own Housing Inventory page says “All owners of residential property are required to report” and adds that most owners must report “even if you are not a landlord.”

But the mechanism is not what the phrase “apply for a licence” suggests. There is no licence application and no approval step. You file the annual Housing Inventory for each unit; the licence for a tenant-occupied unit is then generated automatically. Reporting is free. The Rent Board states plainly: “Landlords are not required to file a petition with the City to impose these types of rent increases” — so an ordinary annual or banked notice goes to the tenant, never to the Board for approval.

The precise timing test (this is the whole ballgame). Adopted Rule §13.14 says the effective date of the increase — not the date you serve the notice — is what decides whether you were licensed. An increase effective while you are unlicensed is “null and void”. Your banking rights survive, so you do not lose the skipped years. Practical consequence: finish the reporting and confirm the licence before you serve, because the safe sequence costs nothing and the wrong one can void the whole increase.

Privacy first: the Housing Inventory submission is public. It can carry the unit address, owner or manager name and business contact, square footage, bed and bath counts and occupancy history. Rent is reported in $250 increments, not exact dollars. See F-18.

blocks.head: The process, step by step — written for someone who has never done this
blocks.body:
Before you do anything else: the only thing standing between you and an unenforceable increase is a licence on the effective date. Here is the whole sequence.

  1. Confirm the unit is covered. Rent control generally attaches to residential units built on or before 13 June 1979 that are not exempt. A reported 1940 build points to coverage, but confirm the parcel on the official Property Information Map and, if unsure, ask a Rent Board counsellor (415-252-4600). F-07, F-08.
  2. Rebuild the rent ledger for each unit. You need the tenancy start date, the lawful starting rent, the date and amount of every increase actually imposed, and the years when an allowed increase was skipped. Banking depends entirely on this. F-05.
  3. Work out the anniversary date. The first annual increase can take effect 12 months after the tenancy began; after that you cannot increase again until 12 months have passed, and the effective date becomes the new anniversary date. F-01.
  4. Report into the Housing Inventory at the Rent Board Portal (free, online, 24/7). Report each unit. The licence for a tenant-occupied unit is then generated automatically. Remember the submission is public. F-18.
  5. Confirm both licences are current in the portal before you serve anything, and screenshot the record.
  6. Calculate the amount. Take the percentage in force on the effective date (not the date you serve), add any banked percentages — added, never compounded — apply the total to base rent only, and do not round up.
  7. Draft the notice. It should state the dollar amount, the percentage, the date it takes effect, and which part of it is banked.
  8. Serve it in time. 30 days for an increase at or under 10%; 90 days above 10%; add 5 more days if you mail it.
  9. Re-check licence status on the effective date and keep the proof with the ledger.
  10. Do not touch the rent while any of this is unresolved, and re-check File No. 261020 before any large banked catch-up.

blocks.head: The one-sentence answer
blocks.body: The 2023 rule is local — San Francisco Administrative Code Chapter 37, §37.15, added by Ordinance No. 265-20, effective 18 January 2021, with the duty reaching condominiums and buildings with fewer than 10 units on 1 March 2023. It is not a state law. The state law you must also obey is the notice rule in Civil Code §827.

blocks.head: How a tenant — or a tenant's lawyer — will test you
blocks.body:
The Rent Board publishes the exact route a tenant uses, and it takes about two minutes. See F-17.

  1. Search the Rent Board Portal by address or Assessor's Parcel Number.
  2. Check whether a Rent Increase Licence existed on the effective date of the increase — the Board's guidance says to “check multiple years for all relevant dates”.
  3. If there was no licence and the increase has not yet taken effect: file a Tenant Summary Petition (Form 518). The Board then sends the landlord a letter saying a licence must be obtained before the increase takes effect.
  4. If it has already taken effect: file a Tenant Petition for Unlawful Rent Increase (Form 516C), which may be set for a hearing before an Administrative Law Judge and can lead to a rent refund.

The licence does not have to be attached to your notice — but that does not help you, because the tenant can look it up anyway.

blocks.head: The 180-day retaliation trap
blocks.body:
Under Civil Code §1942.5(a), if a tenant has (in good faith) given a §1942 notice, complained to the owner about tenantability, complained to an appropriate agency, or if there has been an inspection or citation, the owner may not increase the rent for 180 days from the latest of those events, where the tenant is not in default in rent. Subdivision (d) extends the same protection to tenants who have lawfully organised or participated in a tenants' association. A tenant may invoke §1942.5(a) once in any 12-month period.

Operational consequence: before serving any notice, check whether either household has made a habitability complaint, requested repairs in writing, or contacted an agency in the last six months. If so, the timing of the increase is a legal question, not a business one. See the tenant-lawyer test.

blocks.head: Practical drafting notes that cost nothing and remove the obvious attack lines
blocks.body:
• Use the percentage in force on the effective date, and say which period it comes from.
  • Show the arithmetic on the face of the notice: base rent → percentage → dollar amount → new base rent.
  • Itemise the banked years separately, with the year and percentage each.
  • Do not round up; carry the cents exactly.
  • Do not include pass-through amounts in the base used for the percentage.
  • State the service method and keep proof of service dated on the day you serve.
  • Never reference a tenant's protected characteristic, immigration status, complaint history or tenancy-organising activity anywhere in the notice or in any covering conversation.

blocks.head: What this means for you as a single-building owner
blocks.body:
Three points follow directly from the official text:

  1. You are not exempt and you are not a special case. The ordinance applies to “Owners” with no threshold. If it helps: the Rent Board has said most owners must report “even if you are not a landlord”.
  2. You have one advantage, not a legal one but a practical one. With two units you can evidence your decision unit-by-unit from two short ledgers. A 200-unit owner cannot explain any single increase without a system. Documented, neutral, unit-level arithmetic is the strongest record available to you and it is cheap to produce.
  3. You carry the same exposure as a corporation. 42 U.S.C. §3604 and Government Code §12955 apply to the owner of any housing accommodation regardless of portfolio size. There is no small-landlord carve-out.

pages.title: Raise one unit or both? The discrimination question
pages.desc: 42 U.S.C. §3604 and Government Code §12955 read directly: uniformity is not required, and uniformity is not a defence.
pages.lede: The statutes prohibit treating someone differently because of a protected characteristic. They do not require you to treat every tenant identically, and identical treatment is not a defence if the selection reason is itself unlawful.

blocks.head: So: one unit or both?
blocks.body:
Decide it on the ledgers, not on optics. Under San Francisco's own rules the two units are not similarly situated: Unit B's rent has not moved since 2019 while Unit A's has not moved since 2025, so the banked entitlement diverges sharply. Applying each unit's own lawful maximum is arithmetically explainable and is the single most defensible posture available.

The risk pattern to avoid is not “different numbers” — it is raising the unit occupied by a household with a protected characteristic while leaving an identically situated unit untouched. That is the fact pattern a tenant lawyer looks for, and it is why the reason must be written down before the notice is served, not reconstructed afterwards.

Two cautions specific to this file:

  • Unit B's banked entitlement, if the ledger confirms it, produces an increase above 10% — which triggers the 90-day notice rule and sits above the cap proposed in File No. 261020. Size and timing matter more here than symmetry.
  • If you raise only one unit, write down in one sentence why that unit and not the other, in terms of dates and ledgers only. If you raise both, do the same. The sentence is the evidence.

This site does not promise that any particular choice would survive a lawyer's review. It shows what the statutes prohibit and what the record would need to show.

blocks.head: Current status of those 16 gates on this file
blocks.body:
Gates 1, 2, 4, 7, 9, 13 and 14 cannot be answered from the brief alone — they depend on licence records, ledgers and private facts that were not supplied. Gates 5, 6, 8, 10, 11 and 12 are rules rather than facts and can be satisfied by drafting correctly. Gate 16 is a live risk on Unit B. Gate 3 depends on the reporting you now file. Gate 15 is not triggered on the reported facts because an original occupant remains in Unit A.

Honest summary: on the information available today, this file would not survive an unqualified “done reasonably, normal business practice, no discrimination” sign-off — not because anything was done wrong, but because the licence status and the ledgers are unknown. That is fixable in an afternoon of document retrieval, and the open questions page sets out exactly which documents to pull.

blocks.head: Free, officially verified routes a tenant can use
blocks.body:
• Rent Board counselling, free, 415-252-4600, weekdays 9am-12pm and 1pm-4pm — available to landlords as well as tenants.
  • Tenant Summary Petition (Form 518) if the increase has not yet taken effect and there is no licence.
  • Tenant Petition for Unlawful Rent Increase (Form 516C) once it has taken effect; may be set for a hearing before an Administrative Law Judge and can lead to a rent refund.
  • Portal licence lookup by address or Assessor's Parcel Number, including previous years.

San Francisco's Tenant Right to Counsel programme was not confirmed on an official sf.gov page during this pass — only commercial summaries were found, so it is flagged rather than asserted (F-19).

blocks.head: The decision rule this page implies
blocks.body:
Q-01, Q-02, Q-03, Q-04 and Q-05 are hard blockers. Until the licence status is confirmed, Unit A's anniversary is fixed, and Unit B's ledger is reconciled, the dollar amounts on this site are arithmetic exercises and nothing more. They must not be used to draft a notice.

Q-11 is a timing blocker for Unit B only. A banked catch-up above 10% served while File No. 261020 is pending and drafted to reach notices served on or after 15 September 2026 is a decision that should be made consciously, with advice.

Q-15 and Q-16 are permanently blank by design. They are the two questions where an answer would have to be invented, and inventing one is exactly what this site is built not to do.
